01-38.solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sec\theta - \tan\theta\): \(\frac{\sec\theta - \tan\theta}{(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)(\sec\theta - \tan\theta)} = \frac{\sec\theta - \tan\theta}{\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta} = \sec\theta - \tan\theta\), using \(\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1\). The fact \(\sin\theta = \tan\theta\cos\theta\), while true, plays no role in this proof — the Pythagorean-type identity alone is the reason.

05-47.stem: In a triangle ABC, if \(\sin(A + B) = \frac{3}{4}\) and \(C\) is obtuse, find \(\cos C\).

08-51.stem: Find the number of roots of \(\sin x = \frac{x}{100}\).
08-51.solution: Since \(|\sin x| \le 1\), roots require \(|x| \le 100 \approx 31.83\pi\). For \(x > 0\): one root in \((0, \pi)\), and two roots in each positive hump \((2k\pi, (2k+1)\pi)\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, 15\) (the last hump \((30\pi, 31\pi)\) still lies below 100), giving \(1 + 30 = 31\) positive roots. By symmetry there are 31 negative roots, plus \(x = 0\): total \(31 + 31 + 1 = 63\).
08-51.reason: As printed ('sin x = x/10 in [−10π, 10π]') the answer is 7 — the line x/10 exits [−1,1] at |x| = 10 ≈ 3.2π, so the options 59–65 belong to the classic x/100 variant. Stem repaired to sin x = x/100 (the equation itself confines |x| ≤ 100); key C (63) retained and now correct.
